key_insight: Bacteria with multiple flagella are much better at swimming upstream in flowing fluid because multiflagellarity improves near-wall residence and shear-driven reorientation, not because they swim faster.
engineering_relevance: For biofilm control, infection modeling, and microfluidic design, flagellar architecture can matter more than swimming speed when predicting bacterial transport against flow.
method: Directed evolution and genetics (including flhD/C overexpression)
3D holography, single-cell tracking, and hydrodynamics simulations
evidence_signal: Peritrichous E. coli and S. enterica accumulated upstream at densities up to five orders of magnitude higher than monotrichous P. aeruginosa and V. cholerae, despite Vibrio swimming about three times faster.
watch_item: The conclusions come from controlled microfluidic and simulation settings, so real physiological flows and surface conditions may alter the balance of residence, reorientation, and upstream transport.
